Tac
Hongkong Jan. 5, 1938
Dear Ma;
have just bought myself a Christmas present in the
form of a baby portable type writer which has standard key-
board but weighs only eight pounds and fits in a brief case.
What Hoboken is for the stage - you are for this gadget.
There have been many changes in the whole Chinese sit-
uation as you can well imagine.
Our business was at first en-
tirely disrupted and the future looked decidedly dark. Now we
have been able to work out a "new deal" and things are coming
our way very nicely.
The Minister of Communications who was
especially hostile to us has been dismissed and in his place
there is a new man who is quite
friendly and cooperative. It
appears also as though there will shortly be a change in the
Managing Director of CNAC and that here again we shall get a
much better man than we are now trying to work with.
CNAC is now operating between Chungking - Hankow and
Hongkong with DC-2s (like the plane you flew in to Peiping)
and we have just received some large new flying boats which
on the Yangstze between Hankow and Chungking.
There is a great deal of travel on the upper river now because
the Chinese governmental activities have all been moved to
Chungking.
remain in China in charge of CNAC operations
with headquarters in Hongkong and if there is any China left
with our status more satisfactory than before the trouble start-
ed. Kitsie is in Washington but will shortly leave to join her
I expect to return to Manila and Baguio by the hext
which will also carry this letter.
Debby thinks that
perhaps you may have saved copies of some of my "family letters"
written before you came out to China.
If you have any of these
will you please send them to me by airmail.
Only the ones you
received prior to your own departure for the Orient. There are
probably only a fee such letters but I did not save copies and
will be very grateful if you can locate them either in your own
files or possibly some member of the Bixby family may have a few
put away somewhere.
I think copies were sent to Arthur Hoskins
and there was one letter on military avaiation which I sent to
Phil Love with no copies to the family which I would also like
to have.
Perhaps you could call Phil (his initials are P.R.)
and ask him if he can dig up that letter from his files.
I personally feel that the war has not gone too badly
for the Chinese and that her only chance
the start was to
make the war so costly for the Japanese as to bring about a rev-
olution in Japan. If the Japs had simply taken North China and
most of the sea ports, dug themselves in and then waited for the
Chinese to drive them out,
the latter would have had to attack -
a form of warfare with which they are not familiar - under con-
ditions wholly favorable to the Japanese.
Now however the Japs
followed the Chinese into
the interior where it is almost
impossible to maintain their service of supply, communications
are difficult and long lines must be defended against guerilla
attack - a form of warfare with which the Chinese are familiar
and decidedly potent.
If the Chinese morale will just hold out
for another six months or so you may be surprised at the final
outcome of the present hostilities.
Please do not go to too much trouble about the letters
but I will be very grateful if you can
round up a few and
them to me by airmail to Baguio where I hope to remain for the
next few weeks after you receive this letter.
Lots of love and the best of joss for
1938 and many more years to come!
Taraci
properties.sfomuseum:description: Typewritten letter from Harold M. Bixby to his mother, dated January 5, 1938 in Hong Kong; includes description of status of CNAC operations, [William L.] Bond’s position as head of CNAC operations based in Hong Kong, perspective on the war; mentions Kitsie Bond.
